title: Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) Ciphersuites for Transport Layer Security (TLS)
summary: Adds AES ciphersuites to TLS. At the time, TLS supported ciphers like RC2, RC4, IDEA, DES and triple DES. It was replaced by RFC 5246.

eli5.summary: TLS used older secret-code methods. This lets it also use a newer, stronger one. It has been replaced by RFC 5246.

questions: why is aes better than des
subtitle: Stronger encryption options for secure internet connections

tldr.problem: TLS supported weak encryption algorithms (DES, RC2, RC4, IDEA) that had patent issues or poor performance.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3268 adds new ciphersuites using AES encryption, a stronger and patent-free algorithm, in both 128-bit and 256-bit key lengths.
tldr.outcome: Servers and clients gained a more secure, efficient encryption option for TLS connections. The RFC was later updated by RFC 5246.

today: RFC 3268 was obsoleted by RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2). Modern TLS uses AEAD ciphers like AES-GCM that are more secure and efficient than the CBC constructions defined here.

sections.title: The Need for Better Encryption
sections.content:
Transport Layer Security (TLS) is the protocol that secures internet traffic, from web browsers to email. At the time of RFC 3268, TLS supported several symmetric ciphers for encrypting data: RC2, RC4, IDEA, DES and triple DES. However, each had drawbacks. RC2, RC4 and IDEA were subject to patents or trademark claims, making them legally complicated to use. Triple DES, while reasonably secure, was computationally expensive and slow.

The RFC proposes adding AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) ciphersuites to TLS. AES was the outcome of an open standards process run by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and was published as FIPS 197 in 2001. It is patent-free, efficient and has withstood extensive cryptanalytic attack.
sections.eli5: TLS kept messages secret by scrambling them, but the old scrambling methods had problems: some were patented, and one was very slow. AES is a new scrambling method that is faster, stronger and free to use.

sections.title: The AES Ciphersuites
sections.content:
The RFC defines 12 new ciphersuites, all using AES in CBC (cipher block chaining) mode combined with SHA-1 for message authentication. The ciphersuites come in two groups based on key length: 6 ciphersuites for 128-bit AES and 6 for 256-bit AES. The RFC mentions that AES supports 192-bit keys as well, but the RFC only standardises 128- and 256-bit variants to avoid unnecessary proliferation.

Each of the 12 ciphersuites specifies not only the encryption algorithm but also the key exchange method. Options include RSA (using the server's RSA key for key exchange), various Diffie-Hellman modes (DH_DSS, DH_RSA, DHE_DSS, DHE_RSA) and anonymous Diffie-Hellman (DH_anon). The DHE (ephemeral Diffie-Hellman) variants are especially valuable because they provide forward secrecy: even if the server's long-term key is compromised later, past session keys remain secure.
sections.eli5: The RFC adds 12 new ways for computers to agree on secret codes when they connect. Each way combines AES encryption with a different method of deciding on the secret. Some methods use special keys that only work once, so old conversations stay secret even if the main key is later stolen.

sections.title: Technical Details
sections.content:
Each ciphersuite is identified by a two-byte code. For example, TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA is 0x00, 0x2F and TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA is 0x00, 0x35. All ciphersuites use 128-bit blocks (the amount of data encrypted at once), even though Rijndael, the underlying algorithm, technically supports other block sizes.

The message authentication is performed using SHA-1 in an HMAC construction (described in section 5 of RFC 2246, the TLS 1.0 specification). This means the receiving end can verify that a message was not modified in transit.
sections.eli5: Each ciphersuite has a short code so computers can quickly say which method they want to use. All of them use 128-bit chunks of scrambling, and all check for tampering using a special fingerprint method called HMAC.

sections.title: Security and Risks
sections.content:
The RFC believes the new AES ciphersuites are at least as secure as the older ones they replace. However, particular care is needed with the anonymous Diffie-Hellman variants (DH_anon), which provide confidentiality but no authentication. If authentication is required, the parties must authenticate by other means; otherwise, an attacker can perform a man-in-the-middle attack by impersonating both parties. The RFC recommends that if DH_anon is used, the parties should compute a message authentication code (MAC) over the TLS Finished message and compare them to detect such attacks.

The RFC also notes that research identified a chosen plaintext attack against all CBC-mode ciphersuites in TLS 1.0. This weakness does not affect typical web browsing but may affect other applications. The attack does not compromise key material. The RFC predicts the CBC construction will change in a future TLS revision (which it did in TLS 1.2 and later versions).
sections.eli5: AES is strong, but the anonymous method (where computers do not check each other's identity) can be tricked by someone pretending to be both sides. There is also a subtle attack on scrambling methods like this one, but it does not steal the secret codes.

sections.title: Status and Obsolescence
sections.content: RFC 3268 defined important ciphersuites that many systems adopted in the early 2000s. However, it was obsoleted by RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2), which supersedes TLS 1.0 and introduces new ciphersuite definitions. Modern TLS implementations support AEAD ciphers (authenticated encryption) such as AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305, which are more secure and efficient than the CBC constructions defined here.
sections.eli5: This RFC helped make TLS safer for years, but it was replaced by a better version (RFC 5246) that uses even stronger methods.
